questions.text: Which activities are characteristic of the Design Development phase?

options.text: Initial design exploration and concept development, which typically occurs in the earlier Schematic Design phase
Preparation of detailed construction documents and specifications, which is more characteristic of the Construction Documents phase
Refinement of approved designs, development of cost estimates, and preparation of Design Development documents
On-site observation and construction administration, which are activities associated with the Construction Administration phase

rationale.a: Describes Schematic Design (initial exploration and concept development), not Design Development, which refines already-approved designs.
rationale.b: Describes Contract Documents phase (detailed construction documents and specifications), which follows Design Development.
rationale.d: Describes Construction Administration phase (on-site observation), which occurs during construction, not during Design Development.
rationale.correct: Design Development refines the approved schematic design, develops floor plans and elevations, coordinates structural and MEP systems, refines building dimensions, and develops cost estimates (Statement of Probable Project Construction Cost).
rationale.takeaway: Design Development (typically 20%) refines approved designs into coordinated floor plans, elevations, and systems layouts, culminating in SPPCC cost estimation.

questions.text: An architect is billing for completion of the Design Development phase. Which of the following invoices would be most appropriate in terms of payment documentation?

options.text: Invoice for 20% of total fee without supporting documentation, which may lead to disputes over the completion status of the phase.
Invoice for 20% of total fee with evidence of client approval of Design Development documents
Invoice for 50% of total fee in anticipation of Contract Documents completion, which is premature and not aligned with standard billing practices.
Lump sum invoice for all design phases combined, which lacks transparency and may not reflect the actual progress of work.

rationale.a: Invoices without supporting documentation lack clear basis for payment; milestone-based billing requires evidence of client approval to establish payment trigger.
rationale.c: Invoicing for 50% before Contract Documents are complete violates milestone-based payment principles and anticipates work not yet delivered.
rationale.d: Lump sum invoicing for all design phases defeats the milestone-based payment schedule and prevents clear tracking of phase completion.
rationale.correct: The architect should submit an invoice for 20% (Design Development phase) with documentation of client approval of Design Development documents. This creates a clear basis for payment tied to milestone completion.
rationale.takeaway: Invoice for Design Development must include evidence of client approval of design documents to establish milestone-based payment trigger.

questions.text: What percentage of the total architect fee is typically allocated to the Schematic Design phase under the recommended SPP 202 schedule per the Architect's Guidelines?

rationale.a: Confuses Schematic Design at 10% when the typical allocation is 15%; 10% is not a recommended phase percentage.
rationale.c: Confuses Schematic Design at 20% when 20% is actually the typical Design Development phase percentage.
rationale.d: Overstates Schematic Design percentage; 25% is not a standard allocation for any phase under these guidelines.
rationale.correct: Under the recommended schedule for SPP 202 per the Architect's Guidelines, the Schematic Design phase accounts for 15% of the total architect fee. This is the first phase of the typical five-phase payment schedule.
rationale.takeaway: Schematic Design = 15% of total fee; the recommended phase allocation per the Architect's Guidelines is SD=15%, DD=20%, CD=50%, Bidding=5%, CA=10%.

questions.text: How might payment schedules differ between Design-Bid-Build and Design-Build delivery methods?

options.text: They must remain identical regardless of delivery method per SPP 202, ensuring uniformity across all project types
Design-Build projects often front-load payments to earlier phases due to compressed schedules and early contractor involvement
Design-Build projects always reduce the architect's fee by 50%, which is a standard practice in the industry
Design-Bid-Build eliminates the Bidding Assistance phase entirely, streamlining the process significantly

rationale.a: Ignores the explicit practice that alternative delivery methods may justify different payment allocations than the standard Design-Bid-Build schedule.
rationale.c: Incorrectly assumes automatic fee reduction; Design-Build may shift payment timing, not uniformly reduce total fee by 50%.
rationale.d: Ignores that Design-Bid-Build includes Bidding Assistance (typically 5%); Bidding Assistance is a key part of Design-Bid-Build representing the negotiation and bid evaluation phase.
rationale.correct: While recommended SPP 202 percentages typically apply to Design-Bid-Build projects, alternative delivery methods like Design-Build may justify different allocations, often front-loading payments to earlier phases.
rationale.takeaway: Design-Bid-Build uses standard recommended percentages (15-20-50-5-10); Design-Build and CM at Risk often front-load earlier phases due to compressed schedules and early contractor input.

questions.text: What deliverable marks the completion of the Schematic Design phase and triggers the recommended 15% payment?

options.text: Preliminary sketches with no specific scale, often used to convey initial ideas without detailed dimensions
Schematic designs showing design direction, general layouts, and preliminary spatial planning with client approval
Detailed construction documents ready for bidding, including all specifications and material selections
Final cost estimate from the general contractor, which includes a breakdown of all projected expenses and contingencies

rationale.a: Preliminary sketches lack the specificity and client approval required to mark phase completion; schematic designs must show clear design direction and layouts, not just rough sketches.
rationale.c: Detailed construction documents ready for bidding represent Contract Documents completion, not Schematic Design completion.
rationale.d: Contractor cost estimates occur during or after Design Development, not at Schematic Design completion; schematic completion depends on design deliverables, not cost estimates.
rationale.correct: Schematic Design phase completion is marked by schematic designs showing the design direction, general layouts, and preliminary spatial planning with client approval. This triggers the 15% payment.
rationale.takeaway: Schematic Design completion requires design direction, general layouts, and preliminary spatial planning documents with explicit client approval before the 15% payment is triggered.

questions.text: Which phase receives the largest percentage allocation of the architect fee under the typical SPP 202 schedule per the Architect's Guidelines?

options.text: Schematic Design at 15%
Design Development at 20%
Contract Documents at 50%
Construction Administration at 10%

rationale.a: Underestimates; Schematic Design at 15% is only the first phase and represents minimal effort compared to Contract Documents.
rationale.b: Underestimates; Design Development at 20% involves refinement and cost estimation but is still less effort-intensive than preparing complete construction documents.
rationale.d: Underestimates; Construction Administration at 10% covers site observation and administration but is less effort than the design document preparation phases.
rationale.correct: Contract Documents represents the most effort-intensive phase and typically receives 50% of the total architect fee. This reflects the substantial work required for detailed construction documents.
rationale.takeaway: Contract Documents phase = 50% of total fee, the largest single allocation because it demands the most effort for detailed specifications, drawings, and coordination.

questions.text: A project Owner retains 10% of each payment until final project completion. The total architect fee is 4 million pesos. What total amount will the architect have received by the time Contract Documents are complete, prior to final completion, assuming standard phase allocations?

options.text: 3,060,000 pesos (85% of fee minus 10% holdback of amounts paid)
3,400,000 pesos (85% of fee without any holdback), assuming all phases are completed as scheduled
2,720,000 pesos (85% of fee minus 10% holdback from total), reflecting standard industry practices
2,400,000 pesos (60% of total fee paid directly), based on initial phase completion

rationale.b: Ignores the 10% holdback provision; the architect does not receive the full 85% until final completion when the holdback is released.
rationale.c: Applies holdback incorrectly as 10% of total fee (400,000) instead of 10% of earned amounts (340,000).
rationale.d: Incorrectly calculates cumulative percentage; 60% of 4M = 2.4M, which fails to recognize that the architect has earned and should receive 85% of fee minus the holdback.
rationale.correct: The architect has earned 85% of the total fee by Contract Documents completion (4 million × 85% = 3.4 million pesos). With 10% holdback applied to payments made, the architect receives 90% of earned amounts (3.4 million × 90% = 3.06 million pesos). The holdback (340,000 pesos) is retained until final completion.
rationale.takeaway: With 10% holdback: earned amount at CD = 85% of total fee; amount received = 85% × 90% (which is 76.5% of total fee).

questions.text: What is the recommended percentage of the architect's fee paid during Construction Administration under the typical SPP 202 schedule per the Architect's Guidelines?

rationale.a: Confuses Construction Administration with Bidding Assistance, which is typically 5% of the fee.
rationale.c: Overstates Construction Administration; 20% is the typical Design Development phase percentage.
rationale.d: Confuses Construction Administration with Contract Documents, which represents 50% of the fee.
rationale.correct: Construction Administration typically accounts for 10% of the total architect fee under the recommended schedule. This phase extends from construction start through final completion.
rationale.takeaway: Construction Administration = 10% of total fee; extends from construction start through substantial and final completion with site observation and certification.

questions.text: A project extends its Construction Administration phase for 36 months due to phased construction. The original fee was 3 million pesos (10% = 300,000 pesos for CA). How should the architect address the extended timeline?

options.text: Accept that the original 300,000 pesos covers any duration of Construction Administration, regardless of the extension
The contract should have specified whether additional compensation applies for extended Construction Administration or whether the 10% fee covers the extended period
Request a new contract for the extended period, ensuring all parties agree to the revised terms
Automatically increase the fee by 50% for extended duration, unless otherwise negotiated

rationale.a: Exposes the architect to unlimited work without additional compensation; extended CA timelines should be addressed in contract provisions before the work begins.
rationale.c: Requesting a new contract is reactive and may result in disputes; the original contract should have addressed extended timeline compensation upfront.
rationale.d: Automatically increasing fee by 50% lacks contractual basis; compensation must be negotiated and documented based on actual extended scope and duration.
rationale.correct: Projects extending beyond initial estimates require clear contract provisions. The contract should specify whether the recommended 10% Construction Administration fee covers extended administration or whether additional compensation applies.
rationale.takeaway: Contracts must explicitly specify whether extended Construction Administration (beyond 12–24 months) receives additional compensation or is covered by the standard 10% allocation.

questions.text: An architect has completed Contract Documents and they are ready for bidding. The total fee for the project is 2 million pesos. Based on the recommended schedule per the Architect's Guidelines, how much has the architect been paid through Contract Documents completion?

options.text: 1,000,000 pesos (50% of total)

rationale.a: Calculates only Schematic Design and Design Development (35% cumulative) = 700,000 pesos, instead of including the 50% Contract Documents phase.
rationale.c: Calculates 15+20+50+5 = 90% of 2M = 1,800,000 pesos; Bidding Assistance (5%) is not triggered until after bids are received and contract is awarded.
rationale.d: Uses only the Contract Documents phase (50%) = 1 million pesos, instead of the cumulative percentage through Contract Documents completion (85%).
rationale.correct: Through Contract Documents completion, the architect typically receives 15% (Schematic Design) + 20% (Design Development) + 50% (Contract Documents) = 85% of total fee. For a 2 million peso fee, that is 1.7 million pesos. The Bidding Assistance (5%) is earned upon bidding completion, not upon Contract Documents completion.
rationale.takeaway: Through Contract Documents completion (not yet bidding), cumulative payment is 85% of total fee (15+20+50) according to recommended phase allocations.
